title: Isandro and the Songbook
premise: Wendell Halloran has spent five years rebuilding her life in the coastal town of Greyhaven after a betrayal that sent her ex-partner to prison — a betrayal she helped uncover. For a decade, an anonymous correspondent signing only 'Isandro' has been her pen pal through a secondhand songbook, the one constant voice that never asked her to be brave. When Isandro finally moves in next door, he turns out to be Rafe Ondarza, the younger brother of the man Wendell helped convict, who wrote to her originally to understand his brother's crimes and stayed because he fell for her words. As the autumn festival approaches, their growing love collides with the truth of who they are to each other; when Rafe's identity is exposed by a vindictive local journalist, Wendell must choose between the town's loyalty and her own truth, testifying at a reopened hearing that both clears a wrongful conviction and condemns her own past certainties. In the end, Rafe stays after the last festival train leaves, choosing Greyhaven — and Wendell — over the easy exit.
about_author: Silas Coldharbour is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent twelve years cataloguing lighthouse logs and letters found in decommissioned stations along the northern coast. They write slow-burn romances about people who say on paper what they cannot say aloud.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She counts her safe life: the lighthouse cottage, the part-time novel stalled at chapter nine, the Tuesday letters from Isandro tucked into a songbook. Establishes her fear of exposure since the trial. Emotional beat: contentment built on avoidance, cracked open when a moving van arrives next door.

chapters.title: A Stranger with Familiar Handwriting
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The new neighbor introduces himself as Rafe Ondarza, a carpenter restoring the old boathouse. When he signs for a package, she recognizes the slanted 'z' from ten years of letters. She says nothing, goes home, and shakes. Emotional beat: vertigo — the safest voice in her life now has a face she doesn't trust.

chapters.title: What the Letters Never Said
chapters.summary: Rafe's POV. He knows exactly who Wendell is; finding her was half the reason he came. Flashbacks reveal he began writing to understand his brother Teo's conviction, then couldn't stop. He resolves not to tell her yet. Emotional beat: guilt braided with longing, the first lie already forming.

chapters.title: Salt and Sawdust
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Forced proximity: a storm damages Wendell's fence, Rafe repairs it unasked. Their conversation is stilted until music — she hums a tune from the songbook and he finishes it. Emotional beat: the first real spark, terrifying precisely because it feels like recognition.

chapters.title: Chapter Nine
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Stuck on her novel, she reads her old letters for courage and realizes how much of herself she only told Isandro. She tests Rafe at the harbor café with a detail from the correspondence; he answers too perfectly. Suspicion blooms alongside attraction. Emotional beat: the thrill of being known curdling into dread.

chapters.title: The Festival Committee
chapters.summary: Rafe's POV. The town pulls him into planning the autumn Lantern Festival, and belonging tempts him even as journalist Pru Calloway starts asking why a convicted felon's brother moved to Greyhaven. He deflects, but Pru keeps a folder. Emotional beat: the intoxication of community shadowed by a ticking clock.

chapters.title: Low Tide Confessions
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. On the tidal flats, Wendell tells Rafe a sanitized version of the trial — that she testified against a man who stole from the marina trust. Rafe listens, knowing she's describing his brother, and says nothing. Emotional beat: intimacy deepening on a foundation of mutual concealment.

chapters.title: The Songbook's Margins
chapters.summary: Rafe's POV. Rafe finds the original songbook in Wendell's unlocked cottage while returning a borrowed tool — and discovers her marginalia responding to his letters years before he knew her name. He understands she loved the words before the man. Emotional beat: hope, and the weight of how badly the truth could wound her.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Kiss
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. At the lighthouse during the season's first cold snap, the tension breaks; they kiss. That night Wendell writes a letter to Isandro describing falling for someone else — a message meant for the man standing beside her all along. Emotional beat: joy shot through with dramatic irony.

chapters.title: Pru's Folder
chapters.summary: Pru Calloway's POV (brief) then Wendell's. Pru shows Wendell a photo: Rafe Ondarza, Teo's brother, at the courthouse five years ago. Wendell's world tilts — the letters, the handwriting, the too-perfect answers. Emotional beat: betrayal arriving twice, once in the past and once in the present tense.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She confronts Rafe with the photo. He admits everything except the one thing she can't forgive: that his early letters were reconnaissance. She walks out into the rain. Emotional beat: heartbreak as recognition — she fell for a voice assembled from her own loneliness.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Rafe's POV. Devastated, Rafe re-reads every letter and maps how the correspondence changed him — when the questions became confessions, when Teo's case stopped being the point. He drafts a full confession letter and can't send it. Emotional beat: grief as proof of love.

chapters.title: The Town Takes Sides
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs. Pru publishes a piece framing Rafe as an infiltrator; the festival committee wavers; Wendell's oldest friend Marta urges her to run him out of town for loyalty's sake. Wendell refuses to sign the petition but won't defend him either. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth made communal and public.

chapters.title: Teo's Version
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Rafe leaves her his brother's case file on her porch. Reading it, Wendell finds discrepancies she ignored five years ago — evidence suggesting Teo took the fall for the marina's beloved former harbormaster. Her certainty, the thing her whole rebuilt life rests on, cracks. Emotional beat: horror at discovering justice may have been vengeance.

chapters.title: What I Knew and When
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, flashback-heavy. She reconstructs the trial: the pressure, the town's hunger for a culprit, her own eagerness to be the reliable witness. She realizes she testified to details she never actually saw. Emotional beat: shame transformed into resolve — if she was wrong, only she can unmake it.

chapters.title: The Letter She Writes Back
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She writes to Isandro for the first time since learning his identity — a raw, unsentimental letter telling him she read the file, she believes Teo may be innocent, and she is going to do something about it whether or not he ever forgives her. She leaves it in his mailbox. Emotional beat: courage expressed the only way she trusts, on paper.

chapters.title: Reopening the Case
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Wendell contacts the original defense attorney; Rafe, reading her letter at dawn, comes to the boathouse where she's spread documents across the floor. They work together, awkward and honest, filing for a post-conviction review before the festival. Emotional beat: partnership rebuilt on truth instead of fantasy.

chapters.title: Pressure and Petitions
chapters.summary: Pru's POV and town chorus. Pru threatens to expose Wendell's recantation before the hearing; the harbormaster's family leans on Marta; someone ransacks the boathouse and steals the file. Rafe is nearly arrested on an old warrant Pru dug up. Emotional beat: the cost of justice outside the law, paid in reputation and safety.

chapters.title: Lantern Night
chapters.summary: Climax, part one. At the festival, Pru plans to ambush Wendell on stage; instead Wendell takes the microphone voluntarily and tells the whole town what she got wrong five years ago. The crowd's lanterns dim around her as she speaks. Emotional beat: the novel's thesis enacted — truth offered freely rather than extracted.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Climax, part two. Wendell recants on the record; the stolen file resurfaces via Marta, who chooses truth over loyalty at last; the court vacates Teo's conviction pending retrial, and the harbormaster's crimes come to light. Rafe watches from the gallery. Emotional beat: catharsis — justice done, though no one emerges clean.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Falling action, alternating POVs. Vindicated but exhausted, Rafe prepares to leave Greyhaven — Teo needs him elsewhere, and he assumes Wendell's truth-telling didn't include forgiving him. At the emptying festival platform, Wendell appears with the songbook and asks him to stay. Emotional beat: the blurb's promise fulfilled; choosing each other without illusions.

chapters.title: Everything After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, epilogue. Spring: Teo home and working the boatyard, Marta mending fences, Pru writing a redemption series. Wendell finishes chapter nine of her novel — it's this story — and reads the ending aloud to Rafe in the lighthouse kitchen. Final image: two letters, side by side, no longer needing to be sent. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not granted.
